lesson.title: No Power Required: The Passive Filter
lesson.summary: A passive filter is built entirely from resistors, capacitors, and inductors with no external power source, which keeps it simple and robust but limits it to a gain of one or less and makes its response sensitive to whatever source and load impedances it is connected to.
lesson.body:
Every filter built so far in this chapter, the RC high-pass, the RL low-pass, the RL high-pass, and the RLC band-pass, has been a passive filter. The word passive means the filter is made only from components that store or dissipate energy, resistors, capacitors, and inductors, with no external power supply and no active gain device anywhere in the circuit. That is a direct consequence of what those three components are: a resistor turns electrical energy into heat, a capacitor stores energy in an electric field, an inductor stores energy in a magnetic field, and none of them can add energy to a signal the way an amplifier can.

That simplicity is also the passive filter's main limitation. Because it cannot add energy, a passive filter can never provide gain, at every frequency the output amplitude is at most equal to the input, and usually somewhat less even in the pass band, an effect called insertion loss. There is also a subtler problem: a passive filter's frequency response is not fixed once you pick R, L, and C, it also depends on the impedance of whatever is connected before it (the source) and after it (the load), because those impedances form part of the same voltage divider that sets the filter's response. Connect the same passive filter to a different source or load and its actual cutoff frequency shifts.

Here is a concrete demonstration of that loading effect. Design a simple RC low-pass filter intending R = 3300 ohms and C = 47 nanofarads (4.7 x 10^-8 F), assuming an ideal, zero-resistance source. The nominal cutoff is fc = 1 / (2*pi*R*C) = 1 / (2*pi*3300*4.7e-8). The product R*C = 3300 x 4.7e-8 = 1.551 x 10^-4, so fc = 1 / (2*pi*1.551e-4) = 1 / (9.745 x 10^-4), about 1026 Hz. Now suppose the signal actually comes from a source with 600 ohms of internal resistance, typical of many audio line outputs. That source resistance sits in series with R as far as the filter's RC divider is concerned, so the effective resistance is really 600 + 3300 = 3900 ohms. Recomputing, R_eff*C = 3900 x 4.7e-8 = 1.833 x 10^-4, so the actual cutoff is fc = 1 / (2*pi*1.833e-4) = 1 / (1.152 x 10^-3), about 868 Hz. That is roughly 15 percent lower than the 1026 Hz the designer expected, purely because the filter's own impedance interacts with the source it is connected to. A passive filter has no buffer between itself and the world; it must live with whatever is wired around it.

None of this makes passive filters a poor choice, far from it. They need no power supply, they add no electronic noise, they work at frequencies (well into the radio-frequency range) where active devices struggle to keep up, and they are often the cheapest and most reliable option available. But the loading sensitivity just demonstrated, along with the total absence of gain, are exactly the two problems that the active filter, covered next, is designed to solve.
